definition: A security vulnerability where DNS queries bypass a VPN tunnel and are sent directly to your ISP's DNS servers, revealing your browsing activity despite using a VPN.
metaDescription: Learn about DNS leaks - how they expose your browsing activity even when using a VPN, and why they compromise your online privacy and security.
simpleExplanation: When you use a VPN, all your internet traffic should go through the encrypted tunnel. A DNS leak happens when your device accidentally sends website lookup requests directly to your internet provider instead of through the VPN, exposing what sites you visit.
whyItMatters: DNS leaks defeat the purpose of using a VPN for privacy. Your ISP can still see which websites you're visiting, your government might monitor your activity, and your true location could be revealed to websites and advertisers.
technicalDetail: DNS leaks occur when the operating system's DNS resolver bypasses the VPN tunnel due to misconfigured network settings, IPv6 fallback mechanisms, or transparent DNS proxying by ISPs. This causes DNS queries to be sent to the default gateway's DNS servers rather than the VPN provider's DNS servers.

examples.explanation: A Windows user connects to a VPN but their system continues using their ISP's DNS servers due to network adapter priority settings, allowing their ISP to log all visited websites despite the VPN connection.
A user's VPN only tunnels IPv4 traffic, but their device makes IPv6 DNS queries that go directly to their ISP, revealing browsing activity even though web traffic appears to come from the VPN server.
An ISP intercepts all DNS requests on port 53 regardless of destination, so even when a user configures custom DNS servers through their VPN, the queries are redirected to the ISP's DNS servers.
